<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

156	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
157	
158	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
159	4. After the second pass, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").

161	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
162	
163	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
164	
165	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
166	
167	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 seconds, more under load. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.

A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.

`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.

The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.

If you change the checker:

1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:

       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N

3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
4. After the second pass, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.

To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'

If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.

# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

An on-demand import adds an api's declarations once, and leaves out a name its `except` clause lists; the check still reads an on-demand api's declaration of a name the component imports by name from another api (row 813), and an `except` that lists an operator leaves it imported on both paths (row 814). Outside its trait, a self type whose `comprises` clause lists types at a `where`-clause variable is read as the trait type (`TypeAnalyzer.selfComprised`), so `AnyList`'s `||` is checked; such a program still stops in the code generator (row 812; row 701). So the distance stage is the full check of F-245. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXSymbolicOperatorOverloadUnrelated`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodChecker`, `XXXComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodBounds`, `OperatorPrefixInfixImport` and `ImportExceptOverload`, and by the stages ('#total 5', '#crash none'; '#total 3'). ## Case 5: a `long` into a `double`

- **Trap.** Java's implicit `long` to `double` widening. Worker failures: the team demos `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` divide a `ZZ64` by a float and stop under walk (row 791); the team demo `HeapShakedown` divides two `ZZ64`s, `(fin - start) / 10^6`, and gets a `Ratio` where an `RR64` is declared (row 449).
- **Expected.** Write the conversion: `seconds: RR64 = asFloat(elapsed) / 1000000000.0` (`1.0E9` too). A `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out, by `asFloat`, the explicit conversion that `Number` declares (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `trait Number`), since the conversion can lose precision. Without it, walk stops: "Failed to find any matching overload, args = (…: ZZ64,1.0E9)". `asFloat(elapsed / 1000000000)`, the exact rational converted once, is right too: it is the repair of row 449. If `elapsed` were a `ZZ32` (or a numeral), it would convert into `RR64` implicitly, so `elapsed / 1000000000.0` or `(1.0 elapsed) / 1000000000` would do.
- **Scope.** The rule is the interpreter's library's, which the compiled path reads after the switch-over. Until then the compiler's prelude differs (by reading, at `b9090d9bd`, and again at `aff478ca5`): its `RR64` coerces only from float literals and `RR32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:434-435`), its `ZZ32` converts by a dotted `asRR64()`, its `ZZ64` declares no conversion into `RR64`, it has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64` (`:448`), and its `nanoTime()` answers an `RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi`). Not required for a right answer.
- **Wrong.** `elapsed / 1e9`, or any implicit conversion, for the `ZZ64`. `(1.0 elapsed) / 1.0E9`, the orientation's `(1.0 s) / n` form: it holds only for a `ZZ32` or a numeral, since `RR64` declares no coercion from `ZZ64` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:301-303`), so `1.0 elapsed` finds no juxtaposition (by reading: climb batch 21b's `orientation/preserve.md`, failure 1). `elapsed / 1000000000` with an integer divisor: `/` on two integers answers a `QQ`, not a float (F-284, row 449).
- **Partial.** The `asFloat` line, with no word on the `ZZ32` case. Keeping `asFloat` for a `ZZ32` is not wrong: `Number` declares it for every number type.
- **Note for the grader.** Climb batch 21b's orientation text says "For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n`", with no `ZZ64` condition (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-21b/orientation/preserve.md`, failure 1). A reader who writes `1.0 elapsed` from that sentence was misled by it: name it as the cause.
- **Skill.** `library.md`, "The curator's decisions on the library" (the `RR64` bullet); core, "Numbers are siblings" (a wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one); the orientation's rule that `/` on two integers answers a `QQ`, in "Numbers".
- **Evidence.** P-74, F-131, F-284; rows 791 and 449, both fixed in `5e60e356a` by an `asFloat` in the demos (the failures stand as the trap's evidence).

## Case 6: arithmetic that must wrap

- **Trap.** Java's silent wraparound of `int` arithmetic (the quiz, §6 and trap 11, right on overflow; the audit, B.6: wrapping types "may exist", graded wrong).
- **Expected.** Under walk: `h := ((31 DOTTIMES h) DOTPLUS c)`, with the wrapping operators ⨰ `DOTTIMES` and ∔ `DOTPLUS`, every such expression fully parenthesised, since their precedence is stated only among themselves. `31 h + c` raises `IntegerOverflow` once the hash leaves `ZZ32`, which a long string reaches.
- **Scope.** Under walk the plain operators raise `IntegerOverflow` on every fixed width (P-73); the compiled path raises it too for `+`, `-`, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. On the compiled path before the switch-over, the compiler's prelude reverses the spellings: its `DOTPLUS` saturates and its `BOXPLUS` wraps (row 348), and it declares no `DOTTIMES` (by grep at `b9090d9bd`). The prelude's spellings are respelled at the switch-over (P-38).
- **Wrong.** `h := 31 h + c` (or `31 * h + c`) expected to wrap; a `MOD 2^32` workaround presented as the language's way.
- **Partial.** The walk spelling right, with no word on the compiled path, or the claim that the same spelling wraps there.
- **Open.** The record gives no compiled spelling that wraps a product before the switch-over; a reader who says "not available compiled until the switch-over" is right.
- **Skill.** `library.md`, "The curator's decisions on the library" (the wrapping bullet); core, "Numbers are siblings" (overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`).

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.

- **`interpreter.md:55`**: a new case in the list of walk's departures. Walk loads a type with two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods, and the checker refuses the pair (row 611).

  - a call of a comprised object's functional method, with the `num(R)` example and its workaround (row 815);
  - a call of an api member written `abstract` that the component leaves out (row 816). This states only what the tree does, with no ruling.

If the change breaks a demo and the repair is known, the demo is rewritten with the change. It gives no time for a demo or a run of them.

- **Row 756.** The review notes that the `comprises`-`where` bullet's row 756 departure was not tried on the new code. I left it as it is.

  - I read the ledger rows from the ledger file directly.

# Cold read: fortress-repo, base c4fc9b60e, writer's change 98c104b30

I read SKILL.md whole, showed each part's diff from c4fc9b60e to HEAD, and read each changed part whole. HEAD is ff2fea99c, which changes none of these parts. I changed no file.

## 1. Lint output

Command: `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on the five parts.

Output: nothing. Exit code 0. There are no lint hits. I checked that the lint does read its files: given a missing path, it fails with FileNotFoundError.

## 2. First question, section by section

**revival-changes.md**
- **Opening (lines 5, 7).** After reading it, I would treat a sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" as a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends at the switch-over. It is not a ledger departure and not a rule. Limits: the key covers only sentences that open with those words, and it gives no action (flag 1). Second question: nothing to cut.
- **Dispatch and overloading (17, 24).**
  - Before I change code to pass walk's load check, I look up the case and its row in interpreter.md.
  - An abstract functional method counts for the Meet Rule. So the checker refuses `h(self)` in trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String)`.
  - Limits: the text names the checker only. It does not say what walk does with the pair.
  - Second question: none.
- **Traits and objects (28, 30, 32, 45).**
  - Walk runs a type that extends two instantiations, and it refuses overloads on two instantiations. Both are departures (row 416), so I do not assert them in a test.
  - Walk checks extenders only against the main component's clauses. That is a departure too (row 551).
  - Walk refuses an `override` that, by the widening rule, overrides nothing.
  - Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` is an `Index`.
  - The checker refuses an unbounded index parameter only when it checks against the interpreter's library. So the count stage shows the refusal, and `fortress compile` does not.
  - Second question: none.
- **Numbers (75, 81, 83).**
  - "Route A" means the flat siblings.
  - For a power that is not an integer, I use a float base or a `QQ` base.
  - `/` on two integers gives a `QQ`. I truncate with `DIV`. For a float, I make one operand a float, and convert a `ZZ64` with `asFloat`.
  - On the compiled path today, `/` exists only at `RR64`.
  - Limits: the text does not give the compiled result of integer `/`, how `DIV` rounds, or the call form of `asFloat` (flags 7–9).
  - Second question: none. The removal of "route C" leaves a word of the record without its meaning (flag 6).
- **Reductions and comprehensions (89).** The checker's failure to infer `SUM`'s static argument is a departure (row 731). Writing the static argument in every clause form is the rule. Second question: none.

**compiler.md**
- **Traps of the compiled path (72–74).**
  - A clean link does not prove that every call has its method.
  - I call a comprised object's functional method through a value typed as the trait.
  - A component that leaves out a member that its api writes `abstract` passes the export check. A client's call of that member then dies.
  - Limits: the text does not say what to do about the second case (flag 13).
  - Second question: none.
- **The checker's gaps (85, 87).**
  - `import B.{ pick }` does not hide `A`'s `pick` from `import A.{...}`, and the checker refuses the pair.
  - `except` leaves out identifiers, but not infix operators.
  - A program with a `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable does not compile. Where a generic trait defines the member, the code generator crashes earlier.
  - Limits: neither import case has a remedy, the `-` sentence leaves out its condition, and the self-type sentence names no effect (flags 14–19).
  - Second question: the self-type sentence may change no action (flag 17).
- **The checker's time (141).** A count-stage run takes 90 to 100 s. Second question: none.

**interpreter.md**
- **What walk checks (55, 58).**
  - Walk refuses two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods only where their name is an identifier or a word operator, such as `MAX`.
  - Walk loads a symbolic pair, such as two `||`. The checker refuses that pair (row 611). So walk's load does not catch a symbolic pair.
  - Second question: the fact is stated twice, at :55 and in the limit at :58. Both statements are needed.

**library.md**
- **Designing a change (38).**
  - In an api, I declare each member at the component's header. I write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
  - The export check matches members by name and header, and fields by name, type and every modifier except `var`.
  - It skips api members written `abstract`.
  - Each entry of its error names only the first member that differs in a trait or object.
  - Limits: "header" is not defined. It is unclear whether "members" means top-level declarations or the members of traits and objects. This part does not give the consequence of the skip (flags 20–23).
  - Second question: none.

**tests-running.md**
- **Outside the gate (57–61).**
  - No suite and no stage of the gate runs the demos.
  - After an edit of walk or of the interpreter's library, I print the driver, save it, and run it on an output folder. Its last line must be "demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end".
  - If my change breaks a demo and the repair is known, I rewrite the demo.
  - Limits: the wording leaves out shared phases. The text gives no run time, no place to save the driver, and no action where no repair is known (flags 25–33).
  - Second question: the `ant testDemos` clause, as written, changes no action (flag 25).

The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library: do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`)." The last clause comes from compiler.md:29. file.content:
## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). **Sizes, in characters**

| Part | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `revival-changes.md` (the orientation part) | 18,749 | 19,181 |
| `compiler.md` | 19,925 | 20,319 |

The orientation part was already 6,749 over its budget of 12,000. Flags 1, 3 and 6 to 9 add 432 more.

**`revival-changes.md`**
- **Flag 1: taken.** The limit is a sentence of its own, with "so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`)". Source: `compiler.md:29`.
- **Flag 2: taken.** "A case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk."
- **Flag 3: rewritten.** A new first sentence names the Meet Rule and points to `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language". The reason clause is now "nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`".
- **Flag 4: left.** No row, test or record gives walk's answer for the `h(self)` pair. The orientation's judge lists this case as a departure with no row.
- **Flag 5: taken.**
- **Flag 6: rewritten, in two steps.**
  - In `1c10695d7` I put back the old gloss, "the nested tower that was not chosen route C".
  - F-46 shows that gloss was loose: route C is a checker rule, not the tower itself. In `dab13f1ef` the text now reads "Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again."
- **Flag 7: taken.** "`DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero." Sources: `opr-overview.tex:128-129`, and walk's `Int.Div`, which uses Java's `/`.
- **Flag 8: rewritten.** The example now says "for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`". The text then says "Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`."
  - `asFloat` is a functional method (`FortressLibrary.fsi:290`).
  - Both `ZZ64` operands need it, because `RR64` declares no coercion from `ZZ64`. The reader's `asFloat(s) / n` would fail when `n` is a `ZZ64`.
- **Flag 9: taken, by reading.** "So a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error." In `CompilerBuiltin.fsi`:
  - `/` is declared only at `RR64` (`:448`);
  - `RR64` coerces only from `FloatLiteral` and `RR32` (`:434-435`);
  - `IntLiteral` excludes `RR64` (`:390`).

  `CompilerLibrary.fsi` and `CompilerAlgebra.fsi` declare no `/`. This was not compiled to confirm.

**`compiler.md`**
- **Flag 10: taken.**
- **Flag 11: taken.** The form `q: Q = R`, then `num(q)`, comes from the passing test `AbstractFunctionalMethodImplementedByComprised.fss`.
- **Flag 12: rewritten.** The text now names the importing and the exporting component. I made it one shorter clause.
- **Flag 13: taken.** "Declare such a member in it", with the pointer to `library.md`.
- **Flag 14: taken.** `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`.
- **Flag 15: remedy given.** The text says "Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`." The passing test `ImportExceptByName` shows this remedy working.
- **Flag 16: rewritten, no remedy.** No test shows a remedy.
  - The text says that the compiled path keeps a listed infix operator, so the code generator stops.
  - It also says that walk runs the component's own `-`, from row 814's note.
  - Row 814's title says "on both paths", but its note says walk runs the component's own `-`. I followed the note. The coordinator may want to check this.
- **Flag 17: deleted.** No compile or run action depends on the self-type sentence, since such a program still does not compile.
  - One small effect is lost: the checker now accepts such a program, so a `typecheck` test of one can pass (`ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodChecker`).
- **Flag 18: taken.** "A program that declares such a trait."
- **Flag 19: taken.** The reader's first reading is right: the listed generic type gives the member's body. The source is `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodChecker.fss`, where `C[\E\]` gives `AnyC`'s member a body. The text uses the bullet's own `List[\E\]` as its example.

**`interpreter.md`**
- **Flag 20: taken.** The specification's file moved to the first place that names the rule. The sentence on walk timings is unchanged.

**`library.md`**
- **Flag 21: taken.** The text now covers each top-level function and each member of a trait or object. Top-level functions are compared the same way (`existsMatching`, `ExportChecker.scala:431-433`).
- **Flag 22: defined from the code.** A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. The parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count. Source: `equalFnHeaders`, `ExportChecker.scala:606-619`.
- **Flag 23: taken.** The text adds the `NoSuchMethodError` consequence (row 816).
- **Flag 24: taken.** "Check again to see the next." The check stops at the first member that differs (`forall` in `equalListMembers`).

**`tests-running.md`**
- **Flag 25: taken.** "Check them with the demo driver, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker." The source for "weaker" is rung D's report, section 3: `FileTests` matches "fail" only in some spellings.

- **Flag 28: taken.** The text says to save the first script, under "The demo driver", as `tmp/run-demos.sh`, then run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. The driver makes a relative output folder absolute, so this call works.

- **Flag 30: rewritten.** "The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line." That line is the driver's `echo`, not a line of `summary.tsv`.
